nameStory: The Eastern Cave Long-jawed Spider gets its name from its favorite hangout spots - the cool, dark entrances and twilight zones of caves and rocky overhangs. The 'long-jawed' part refers to the extended chelicerae (pronounced 'kuh-LISS-er-eye') - those are the mouthparts that look like tiny pincers jutting forward from their face. This spider is perfectly adapted for life in the shadows where most other orb weavers wouldn't dare to spin.
description: This medium-sized spider is a master of dim, sheltered spaces throughout New England. Cave Long-jawed Spiders have elongated bodies with prominent forward-projecting mouthparts that give them an almost prehistoric appearance. They're skilled web builders, creating circular orb webs like their garden spider cousins, but prefer the protected environments of cave mouths, rocky overhangs, and deep forest crevices. Adults typically reach about half an inch in body length, with legs that can span nearly two inches.

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Found in cave entrances, rock crevices, and deep forest overhangs where the air feels noticeably cooler and damper than surrounding areas

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Elongated abdomen and distinctly long, forward-projecting mouthparts (chelicerae) that stick out like tiny antennae from the front of the head

idTips.label: Web
idTips.description: Circular orb web with sticky spiral threads, often positioned vertically in the dim transition zones between light and dark areas

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Body length reaches about half an inch, with total leg span approaching two inches - noticeably larger than most cave-dwelling spiders

idTips.label: Markings
idTips.description: Muted brown to grayish coloration that blends seamlessly with cave walls and weathered rock surfaces

habitat: Look for these spiders in the twilight zones of New England's limestone caves, granite overhangs, and deep rocky crevices throughout the region's mountainous areas. They favor the transition areas where natural light fades but doesn't completely disappear - places that feel cool and humid even on hot summer days. You'll also find them under large boulder formations and in the deepest recesses of old stone foundations where the environment stays consistently moist.

seasonality.spring: Adults become active as cave temperatures stabilize, beginning to build webs in their preferred dim locations. Look for fresh webs appearing in cave mouths and rocky overhangs.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when webs are most visible and well-maintained. Adults are actively hunting and mating during warm months when flying insects venture into cave entrances.
seasonality.fall: Mated females may be seen with egg sacs, and webs remain active as long as temperatures stay moderate. Activity begins to slow as insects become scarce.
seasonality.winter: Adults typically overwinter in deep crevices, remaining relatively inactive. Webs are abandoned, and spiders retreat to the most protected areas of their cave habitats.

funFact: These spiders are living flashlights for cave ecosystems! Their webs act as the primary food collection system for many cave communities - when insects get caught, the nutrients eventually cycle through the entire underground food web, feeding everything from cave crickets to salamanders.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other long-jawed orb weavers that build webs near water sources, but those species prefer bright, sunny stream edges while Cave Long-jawed Spiders specifically seek out dim, protected areas. Remember: if you can comfortably read a book where you find the web, it's probably not a Cave Long-jawed Spider!
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'cave' spiders, they don't actually live deep inside caves where it's completely dark - that's a common misconception. They're really 'cave entrance' specialists that need some filtered light to thrive, making them more accessible to nature explorers than true cave-dwelling species.
compareHints: Since this is the only Meta species commonly found in New England, compare it with other long-jawed orb weavers in the family Tetragnathidae. Unlike stream-loving Tetragnatha species that prefer bright waterside locations, Cave Long-jawed Spiders specifically seek dim, rocky environments. Their habitat preference is the easiest way to distinguish them - if it's in a cave entrance or deep overhang, you've likely found Meta ovalis.
